text.p: A regional sanctions committee on Burundi ended its meeting on Thursday, saying it would pass on its undisclosed recommendations to regional foreign ministers.

Major-General Mirisho Sarakikya, the committee chairman and Tanzania's high commissioner (ambassador) to Kenya, told Reuters the committee had also considered a request to allow foreign journalists to fly into landlocked Burundi instead of getting there by land.
He said the committee will consult on the issue with media and aid agencies who operate flights into the tiny central African state.
"I will be convening a meeting between myself, the media and aid agencies to sort out this matter which the committee felt was purely of an administrative nature," Sarakikya said.
Last week journalists asked the committee to exempt the media from an economic and transport blockade imposed by East African states on Burundi after a July 25 military coup.
The journalists argued they should be permitted to charter aircraft direct from the Kenyan capital Nairobi or Kigali to avoid the risk of being ambushed on Burundi's treacherous northern roads.
Sarakikya said journalists were not covered by the embargo and his proposed meeting would help clear out current misunderstandings and define modes of operation.
U.N. officials have repeatedly said they needed the committee's approval before U.N. agencies could transport journalists on Burundi-bound planes.

"The U.N. did not intend to allow journalists on its planes until the Sanctions Committee said it would let journalists fly," Ben Parker, a spokesman with the U.N. department of humanitarian affairs told Reuters in Nairobi.
The sanctions committee is made up of Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Uganda, Zaire and Zambia as well as representatives of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).

Burundi is the scene of a war between the country's Tutsi-dominated army and rebels of the Hutu majority who have stepped up a military campaign for a greater political stake in their ethnically divided country.
